newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Philips Q3 profit seen sharply lower.
newsitem.headline: Philips Q3 profit seen sharply lower.

text.p: Philips Electronics NV is set to unveil a sharp fall in net profit from normal operations when it reports third quarter results next Thursday, suffering from price erosion and flagging markets, say analysts.

Analysts forecast a drop in net from normal operations to between 240 million and 360 million guilders, a long way behind 539 million in the third quarter of 1995. A decline would mark Philips' third consecutive quarter of reduced profit.
Analysts said Philips continued to be hobbled by slack European demand, particularly for its core consumer electronics products, as well as persistent downward pressure on prices.

The company's warning on October 14 that, based on preliminary third quarter information, second half operating profit was unlikely to improve, caused some analysts to cut their forecasts for third quarter 1996.

"We've downgraded it even more from our earlier forecast based on the extremely limited amounts of information we've had from Philips this week," said ING analyst Steven Vrolijk. "Things are going a bit worse than expected," he said.
For the third quarter Vrojlik was now expecting net income from normal operations of around 288 million guilders, down from his prior forecast of 425 million.
Marc Langeveld at Kempen & Co is forecasting 336 million guilders net profit from ordinary operations.

"336 is a decline of around 38 percent. OK, it could be slightly more but it doesn't change my view for next year or for fourth quarter results. 1996 will be a poor year," he said shortly after Philips' profit-warning.

Many in the markets are steeling themselves for an extraordinary charge as the company's newly installed chairman Cor Boonstra gets to grips with Philips' cost base. A big extraordinary charge could push Philips into an overall net loss, as did a 760 million guilder charge in the second quarter.
Philips took the second-quarter charge to pay for the restructuring which aimed to cut 6,000 jobs over 18 months from the Sound & Vision unit.

"I expect one (restructuring charge) because I think the reorganisation they announced at the second quarter of Sound & Vision was insufficient. I think in some parts of the organisation they need to cut back on personnel costs," said Frits de Vries at Theodoor Gilissen.
